claims.text: Overall, the use of Facebook is negatively associated with well-being.
A 1-standard-deviation increase in likes clicked, links clicked, or status updates is associated with a decrease of 5% to 8% of a standard deviation in self-reported mental health.
The negative associations between Facebook use and well-being are robust to multivariate cross-sectional analyses and 2-wave prospective analyses.
The negative associations of Facebook use are comparable to or greater in magnitude than the positive impact of offline interactions.

evidence.description: Our results showed that overall, the use of Facebook was negatively associated with well-being.
a 1-standard-deviation increase in 'likes clicked', 'links clicked', or 'status updates' was associated with a decrease of 5%-8% of a standard deviation in self-reported mental health.
These associations were robust to multivariate cross-sectional analyses, as well as to 2-wave prospective analyses.

The negative associations of Facebook use were comparable to or greater in magnitude than the positive impact of offline interactions, which suggests a possible tradeoff between offline and online relationships.

methodologies.name: Longitudinal survey and objective social media measurement
methodologies.description: Assessed associations of online and offline social activity with subjective well-being measures using 3 waves of survey data combined with objective Facebook activity metrics.
